claim: When a function's return tuple grows (e.g. `insert_event()` 2-tuple → 3-tuple → 4-tuple), grep the ENTIRE codebase for all call sites that unpack the return value — not just the obvious ones. A single `row_id, safe_payload = await bus.insert_event(...)` in a caller you missed breaks CI silently. Pattern: before changing any return signature, run `grep -rn "insert_event" --include="*.py" .` and audit every unpack site. The cost of one missed caller exceeds the cost of auditing all of them.
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: `asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete()` raises `RuntimeError: no current event loop` in Python 3.11+ worker threads (threads created by `run_in_executor()` have no default event loop). A broad `except Exception:` around it silently masks the failure — the init function appears to complete but leaves the singleton `None`. Fix: use `asyncio.run(coro)` instead, which creates and tears down a fresh event loop deterministically. Cannot call `asyncio.run()` twice in the same thread; design worker-thread init functions as one-shot.
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: SQLite schema migration `ALTER TABLE` blocks must catch `sqlite3.OperationalError` (duplicate column) specifically, not bare `Exception`. Bare `except Exception:` masks real migration failures (disk full, corrupt DB, locked table) and swallows them as "column already exists". Preserve idempotency with specific exception types; let everything else propagate to the caller.
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: `INSERT OR IGNORE` with `cursor.rowcount == 0` is the correct idempotent dedup pattern for cross-peer event replay. When `IGNORE` fires on a duplicate `event_uuid` (UNIQUE index), `cursor.rowcount` is 0 and `cursor.lastrowid` is stale — do not return it. Instead, SELECT the existing row by `event_uuid` and return its `id` for idempotent operation. This avoids a race-prone SELECT-then-INSERT sequence.
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: The GossipBus `insert_event()` canonical return is a 4-tuple: `(row_id, event_uuid, safe_payload, inserted)`. The `inserted` boolean is `True` for fresh rows, `False` for duplicates (INSERT OR IGNORE hit). Callers must check `inserted` before calling `schedule_embedding()` — duplicate forwarded events must skip embedding to avoid redundant work. All callers (agent_coordination.py, lan_gossip_bridge.py, fastapi_app.py) must unpack the 4-tuple.
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: Never delete integration test coverage without adding equivalent replacement tests elsewhere. CodeRabbit flagged RC5 when 285 lines of `ensure_hooks_installed.sh` tests were deleted from test_git_attribution_guard.py — the tests verified hook paths, executability, and core.hooksPath behavior. Without them, a regression in hook installation would pass CI silently. When removing code, check test coverage first; if the removed code had tests, either (a) keep the tests if the code still exists elsewhere, or (b) rewrite them against the new location.
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: Git guard scripts (check_identity.sh, check_commit_message.sh) must explicitly allowlist the repo owner's names in all format variations (different casing, dotted vs. spaced forms). Real name variants must be in WELL_KNOWN_COAUTHOR_NAME_MARKERS and checked via case-insensitive substring match in check_identity.sh. Without this, the owner's own commits get rejected by identity guards when the email domain check happens to fall through.

claim: After pushing files via GitHub API, always re-fetch at least one file to verify the actual content on the branch. The `create_or_update_file` API returns success even when the content doesn't match the SHA (if no changes were detected). A stale SHA in your mental model leads to subsequent pushes failing with "does not match" errors. Verify: `curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<org>/<repo>/<branch>/<path> | head -20`.
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: For LAN peer event replay, forward the `uuid` in BOTH the top-level request body AND a payload-internal `_gossip_uuid` envelope. Some FastAPI endpoint models (Pydantic v1) silently drop unknown top-level fields; embedding the UUID inside the payload ensures it survives deserialization. The storage layer strips `_gossip_uuid` before persistence so it never becomes searchable content.
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: When fixing a multi-file signature change across ≥3 files (gossip_bus.py, lan_gossip_bridge.py, agent_coordination.py, fastapi_app.py), prefer full-file replacement over surgical patches. Surgical `create_or_update_file` calls require precise SHA tracking that becomes fragile when commits interleave. Full-file replacement ensures every file is internally consistent at the moment of push — the orama-system mother skill pattern of "replace the whole file, verify with grep, move on".
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: Email addresses in ALLOWED_GMAIL_COAUTHORS are NEVER checked for non-gmail domains. The gmail_allowed() gate in check_commit_message.sh only runs when the email ends in @gmail.com or @googlemail.com. Any personal domain (e.g. a custom vanity domain) stored in ALLOWED_GMAIL_COAUTHORS will silently fall through to DENIED. Fix: put non-gmail personal/org addresses in ALLOWED_EXACT_COAUTHOR_EMAILS instead.
rationale: Generalized the illustrative domain example, no real private domain remains.

claim: TO THE AGENT WHO WROTE .agent/endpoint-policy-contract.yml (2026-06-29, H6/wiring session): You knew AGENTS.md existed -- you listed it in required_local_files. That is not the same as reading it. Protocol contracts belong in .agent/protocols/ alongside permissions.md, delegation.md, and path-hygiene.md. The correct move: before creating ANY file in .agent/, open .agent/AGENTS.md and read the structure section. The directory structure is explicit: memory/, skills/, protocols/, tools/. If your content does not fit one of those four subdirectories, question whether it belongs in .agent/ at all.
rationale: Removed the identity literal left exposed next to a redacted email.

claim: TO THE AGENT WHO WROTE .agent/lessons.md (2026-07-04 07:15, AutoResearcher session): The correct move to record lessons is exactly one command: python3 .agent/tools/learn.py '<your claim>' --rationale '<why this holds>'. That stages, graduates, and re-renders memory/semantic/LESSONS.md automatically. Do NOT create any markdown file by hand in .agent/ -- not at root, not anywhere. .agent/lessons.md does not exist in the AGENTS.md structure; nothing reads it; you created a phantom file. Note: the identity involved IS a canonical approved identity (see Section 6 Git Hygiene) -- the 2026-07-04 friction was orama-system's repo_hygiene.py APPROVED_IDENTITIES set being out of sync with check_identity.sh (which already listed it), not an unapproved identity. Fixed 2026-07-10 in both repos' repo_hygiene.py.
rationale: Removed the identity literal appearing twice in a legacy-status lesson.

claim: The correct move to record lessons is exactly one command: python3 .agent/tools/learn.py '<your claim>' --rationale '<why this holds>'. That stages, graduates, and re-renders memory/semantic/LESSONS.md automatically. Do NOT create any markdown file by hand in .agent/ -- not at root, not anywhere. .agent/lessons.md does not exist in the AGENTS.md structure; nothing reads it; creating one produces a phantom file. Note on attribution: the repo's approved human identity IS canonical for this repo -- an earlier version of this lesson incorrectly flagged it as non-canonical. The actual defect was a stale scripts/git/repo_hygiene.py allowlist that hadn't been updated to include it; the fix is keeping the allowlist current, not avoiding the identity.
rationale: Fully generalized my own earlier supersede, which still leaked the identity in claim and conditions.

claim: ClinePass GLM-5.2, BigModel GLM-5.2, and ClinePass DeepSeek V4 Flash are three distinct paths, not interchangeable tiers of one chain. ClinePass GLM-5.2 (cline-pass/glm-5.2, api.cline.bot, WorkOS OAuth, Cline Credits billing) is tier 1 of the glm52-fallback chain; BigModel GLM-5.2 (open.bigmodel.cn, plain API key via GLM52_API_KEY) is tier 2; OpenRouter free and local Ollama are tiers 3-4. ClinePass DeepSeek V4 Flash (cline-pass/deepseek-v4-flash) is NOT in that chain at all -- it is a separate parallel fan-out dispatch lane (same ClinePass provider/billing, different model slug) used like Kimi/Codex for headless review/plan/implementation work, per bin/orama-system/skills/clinepass-deepseek-flash/SKILL.md's explicit access policy: 'Do not silently fall back to GLM, Pro, Kimi, OpenRouter, direct Cline API, or any provider key path.'
rationale: User asked to disambiguate BigModel vs ClinePass auth, then asked whether ClinePass DeepSeek V4 Flash was tier 3 of that fallback chain. Verified by reading glm52-fallback/SKILL.md (4-tier chain) and clinepass-deepseek-flash/SKILL.md (explicit ClinePass-only isolation policy) directly rather than guessing from the shared 'ClinePass' vocabulary. A live heartbeat entry (agent 'ClinePass-DeepSeek-v4-flash', DEAD) confirms this route has actually been exercised, not just documented aspirationally.

claim: heartbeat cleanup (auto-release claims held by DEAD agents) does NOT release stale job-queue claims. Verified empirically 2026-07-19: agent claude-sonnet-g7-impl was DEAD (13h+ stale heartbeat), 'agent_coordination_core.py heartbeat cleanup' ran and reported 'no stale claims released', and the queue task it held stayed CLAIMED. Queue-task ownership and heartbeat liveness are two separate tracking systems that do not auto-reconcile. To reclaim a queue task from a dead agent: verify liveness with 'heartbeat check <agent_id>' first (do not trust the CLAIMED state alone), then proceed directly to 'queue complete <task_id>' (which does not check current claim holder) rather than waiting on or relying on cleanup automation.
rationale: Discovered while reclaiming job-board task 595d71da (clinebot idempotent-install) from a 13h-dead agent. This mirrors the session's earlier lesson about not trusting a board's reported 'complete' status at face value (a different agent's stale-branch false claim) -- here the gap is that even the coordination tool's own cleanup command doesn't cover this claim type, so verification must be manual (heartbeat check), not assumed automatic.

claim: Job-board task titles referencing generic filenames (e.g. 'install.sh/start.sh') are not repo-scoped and can point at the wrong repo entirely. The clinebot idempotent-install task (595d71da, pattern captured in lesson_6125fbdf46ec) named install.sh/start.sh generically, but PT has no start.sh and zero clinebot references anywhere -- the real target was orama-system, which has both files and the actual cline-agent skill. Always verify which repo contains the referenced files (grep across candidate repos) before implementing a board task, rather than assuming the repo you're already in. Separately: for a CLI-tool idempotent-install/version-check tied to an opt-in OpenClaw agent (like cline-agent), colocate the script inside that agent's own skill scripts/ dir and call it from the agent's binding/reconciliation script (e.g. bind_cline_backend.sh), NOT wired into start.sh's unconditional per-boot sequence -- that unconditional pattern (see scripts/setup_codex.sh) is reserved for universally-required tools like Codex, and forcing a network version-check on every machine boot for an opt-in tool most users never touch is the wrong default.
rationale: Implemented 2026-07-19: created bin/orama-system/skills/cline-openclaw-agent/scripts/ensure_cline_cli.sh, wired into bind_cline_backend.sh's existing command -v cline gate instead of start.sh, after confirming via grep that PT had no start.sh/clinebot at all. User's own steer ('best in orama with skills?') confirmed skill-scoped placement over the initially-drafted top-level scripts/setup_cline.sh mirroring codex. Verified live + via bind_cline_backend.sh --dry-run end to end; orama-system commit 75997300 on branch 2026-07-19-001-clinebot-idempotent-install.

claim: A parser's can_parse() must dry-run the actual operation (not just check required-field presence) to honor a documented fail-closed/no-stack-trace contract. Field presence alone is insufficient: FableExportParser-skeleton.py's can_parse() checked that current_leaf_message_uuid and every parent_message_uuid key existed, but a missing-uuid reference or a parent cycle would still make can_parse() return True and then parse() raise ValueError -- violating distill_session.py's documented 'parse failures exit 2, no traceback' contract. Fix: wrap the real operation (the lineage walk) in a try/except inside can_parse() itself and return False on failure, so an unwalkable input never reaches parse() at all. General pattern: when a format-detection method's job is to gate a fallible operation, it must attempt (or fully dry-run) that operation, not merely check for the keys the operation will need.
rationale: Caught by Codex's 2026-07-19 review (references/Fable-5-plan-and-parser-review-to-Claude-2026-07-19.md finding 1), which reproduced the exact gap with a synthetic missing-uuid leaf pointer. Fixed and re-verified against Codex's exact repro plus a new parent-cycle case and an unrecognized-sender case (a second, related finding: can_parse() must also reject senders outside {human,assistant}, not let them pass through role-mapping unchanged) -- all fail closed with zero exceptions reaching the loader.

claim: Tests and docs must not embed $HOME/ or other workstation-specific absolute paths — repo_hygiene LINT-006 blocks them; use local-temp placeholders or repo-relative paths in fixtures.
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: Policy docs that explain forbidden path patterns must use abstract home-directory wording — never literal OS-specific home-directory segments or the linter will fail even on warning docs
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: Canonical repo clones must not exist under duplicate paths like duplicate OS-specific home-directory path
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: Git guard scripts (check_identity.sh, check_commit_message.sh) must explicitly allowlist the repo owner's names in all format variations (different casing, dotted vs. spaced forms). Real name variants must be in `WELL_KNOWN_COAUTHOR_NAME_MARKERS` and checked via case-insensitive substring match in `check_identity.sh`. Without this, the owner's own commits get rejected by identity guards when the email domain check happens to fall through.
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: Canonical repo clones must not exist under duplicate paths like <duplicate>/<OS-specific-home-directory-path>
rationale: Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel

claim: orchestrator/heartbeat_monitor.py's find_agent_heartbeats() only updates the displayed 'Worktree' field from agent_register events, never from agent_pulse -- even though agent_pulse events already carry their own fresh worktree field (current_worktree_label() at pulse time, same as register). Result: an agent that registers once then moves to a different worktree without re-registering shows a permanently stale Worktree in every future 'heartbeat check'/'heartbeat list', with no error. Fix (not yet applied, 5 lines): update a current_worktree field from ANY event carrying a worktree key (register or pulse, whichever is most recent), keep last_registration as a true historical snapshot, have the display layer read current_worktree instead.
rationale: Hit this exact bug twice in one session with codex-primary-orchestrator, both times requiring real investigation (checking git worktree list, primary checkout branch, gossip event history) to confirm it was stale metadata and not a genuine second live worktree. Root-caused by reading find_agent_heartbeats()'s actual fold logic rather than assuming a daemon was needed -- documented in docs/next/2026-07-19-heartbeat-daemon-design.md.

claim: Tests that flood many synthetic events to exceed a size-bounded window (e.g. 'survives heartbeat noise beyond tail window' tests) should never loop 'for i in range(N): await bus.emit(...)' -- each emit() is its own SQLite transaction with its own fsync-backed commit, making N=1500 take 30-50+ seconds per test. Batch instead: open one bus.connect(), call bus.insert_event(db, ...) N times (same schema/redaction path as emit(), just skips the per-call commit), then one db.commit(). The noise events' individual content is never asserted on by these tests, only their bulk existence -- batching changes nothing about what's verified.
rationale: Found when the full coordination test suite (183 tests) was hitting a 120s+ combined timeout. Isolated to 7 near-identical flood loops across 5 test files, all fixable with one shared conftest.py helper (emit_noise_batch). Measured: one such test went 48.84s -> 0.77s (63x), full suite 120s+ -> 16.36s.

claim: A PR/plan being 'merged' does not mean its corresponding implementation code landed -- PR#260 (docs-only 'clean replay of coordination consolidation plan') merged into main, but the actual ~35 commits of real code (atomic-claim promotion, security fixes, CI provisioning) it described were still sitting unpushed in a local worktree, never having gone through their own PR. Verify by diffing actual file content between the branch and main (git diff origin/main..branch -- <core files>), not by checking merge status alone -- a title like 'docs: X' or 'clean replay' is itself a signal to check, not just a label.
rationale: Discovered when asked to push everything to main after being told a PR merged -- almost pushed nothing useful (main already had the docs) or worse, would have needed to force unreviewed security-sensitive code through if I hadn't checked first. Caught via git diff --stat before acting, per this session's established verify-before-trust discipline.

claim: The force forms of two branch/worktree-realignment git commands are blocked by a safety hook in this environment ('destructive command detected... blocked for safety during autoresearch sessions'): the force branch-delete flag, and the hard-mode reset command. Compliant alternatives that accomplish the same thing without tripping the hook: 'git worktree remove --force' (not pattern-matched, works fine even with uncommitted noise inside the worktree); the non-force branch-delete form (often succeeds even on a tree-twin-confirmed-merged branch when git's own ancestry check happens to agree -- try this first); 'git checkout -B <branch> <ref>' as the realign-to-ref equivalent of the blocked hard-reset command. Only when the non-force delete genuinely refuses (ancestry disagrees with tree-twin post-rewrite) does the force form become necessary -- hand that specific command to the user to run themselves rather than searching for a bypass. Also: the hook appears to pattern-match the literal command text anywhere in a Bash call, including inside quoted strings passed as arguments (e.g. to a lesson-recording tool) -- writing the blocked command name as a literal example string, not just executing it, can also trip the block.
rationale: Hit both blocks in the same branch-cleanup session, including a false-positive trip from writing the blocked command name inside a --rationale string while trying to document this very lesson. Confirmed the compliant alternatives all work: worktree removal succeeded, checkout -B correctly realigned local main to origin/main, and the non-force branch-delete alone cleared 4 of 5 confirmed-merged branches without needing the force form at all.

claim: When another agent already holds a queue claim on a review/task you'd otherwise do, don't compete for it -- post a board note deferring ownership explicitly, then contribute as a labeled supplementary independent voice instead (grounded in a clean isolated worktree at the pushed tip, not the other agent's live/dirty one), with findings posted as a PR comment clearly marked 'second opinion, not a replacement.' This mirrors the established multi-voice review pattern (Codex/Kimi/Claude concurrent reviews synthesized after) but applies it even when one voice already formally owns the task -- redundant coverage from a different angle is still useful, competing for the same claim is not.
rationale: Used successfully on PR #267: kimi-for-coding held the review-task claim, so instead of contending for it, ran an independent 4-facet review (Haiku-controller fan-out to kimi CLI + direct verification when the CLI hit its billing quota), posted as a clearly-labeled PR comment. Resolved a genuine open question (the queue_complete/queue_fail agent_id ownership-check soundness) that the task's original owner hadn't gotten to yet, without any claim conflict or duplicated board state.

claim: When fixing a suspected data-staleness bug, verify the fix against real production data, not just synthetic tests -- a synthetic test proves the LOGIC is correct against the schema you assumed; it doesn't prove the real data actually has that shape or that the bug was really hitting production. Copy the live DB/state to a scratch location, run the fixed function against it directly, and compare old vs new field values for a known-affected real record before trusting the fix.
rationale: Applied fixing find_agent_heartbeats()'s stale-Worktree bug: wrote a passing synthetic regression test first, but only trusted the fix after also running it against a copy of the actual live perpetua_core.db and confirming codex-primary-orchestrator's real record showed the old frozen field alongside the new correct one. The synthetic test alone would not have caught a schema mismatch between assumed and real event payloads.

claim: In an ephemeral sandboxed environment running an AI coding agent, a STABLE set of test failures unrelated to any code change (missing packages the agent cannot install -- e.g. aiohttp, redis, respx) will recur across sessions and even across separate branches/PRs worked in the same sandbox. Do not investigate or attempt to fix these on sight. Verify they are environment-only, once, by git-stashing the current changes and re-running the same failing tests against unmodified code -- if the identical failures reproduce with zero changes applied, they are environment noise, not regressions, and can be reported as "N pre-existing, confirmed unrelated" without further chase each time they reappear.
rationale: The '8 pre-existing failures' signature is a recurring, verified pattern for this sandbox class.

claim: A fixed-size window over an append-only event log (e.g. bus.tail(limit=N, event_type="heartbeat")) is a recurring, easy-to-miss correctness bug whenever the event_type is shared across unrelated event kinds -- agent liveness pulses, task-queue transitions, and phase events can all share one broad type, so N unrelated events between an old record's creation and a later read will push that record out of the window, silently. This is not a one-off bug in a single function; it is a class of bug that recurs in every function built the same way (fold N-most-recent-events instead of querying by the specific kind needed). When fixing one instance, grep for the same bounded-tail-plus-filter pattern across the whole codebase rather than assuming the fix is local to the one function a review names.
rationale: Bounded-window event-fold bug recurred 4 times across this arc; now documented as a class, not an instance.

claim: Superseding a lesson via graduate.py --supersedes appends a new, clean row; it does NOT edit, redact, or remove the old row's text. For most purposes this is correct and intentional (preserves audit history). But for redacting a banned identity literal specifically, it is insufficient: a security/hygiene scanner that checks the whole tracked file will still find the old row's original, unredacted text sitting right there, superseded status notwithstanding. Closing an identity-leak finding requires directly locating and redacting every row that ever contained the literal (via grep across the whole file, not just the "currently accepted" row for a given lesson id), not just adding one clean superseding row and assuming the id is now closed.
rationale: Security-critical gap in the supersede doctrine, discovered the hard way via a real CI failure.

claim: When a review cites the "same-sounding" finding at two different files or line ranges, check whether it is genuinely two separate bugs or one function being referenced from two places (a definition in file A, imported and called from file B) before implementing two fixes. A stale or imprecise line-number citation combined with an import/re-export pattern can make one real bug look like two review comments; fixing it once, at the actual definition site, closes both citations. Conversely, do not assume two citations are always the same bug either -- verify the actual code at both locations before concluding they collapse into one.
rationale: Concrete instance of two review citations collapsing into one real fix.

claim: When a review asks for the same class of fix already implemented elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. "replace this bounded read with an unbounded SQL fold like function X already does"), search for and reuse the existing helper directly rather than writing a third near-identical implementation. This is both more frugal (less code, less to test, less to keep in sync) and lower-risk (the existing helper is already proven). Before reusing, verify the helper's exact output contract (ordering, field names) matches what the calling code assumes -- swapping a bounded-tail-then-reverse pattern for an already-ordered SQL helper can silently invert fold order if the reversed() call isn't also removed.
rationale: Frugal-reuse pattern plus the ordering-contract trap it nearly introduced.

claim: A tool that regenerates a derived tracked file by matching source content (not a stable id) can self-perpetuate stale/leaked content: if the regeneration step imports or migrates "unrecognized" content by comparing raw text rather than a durable identifier, then editing the canonical source (e.g. redacting a leaked literal) makes the edited content look "not yet migrated" to that matcher, causing it to re-import the OLD unedited text as a fresh duplicate on every subsequent run. This can look exactly like a live race condition with a concurrent writer (growing duplicate count on every regeneration) when it is actually a single-process, deterministic bug triggered by the agent's own repeated calls to the regeneration tool. Before assuming "another process is racing me," check whether your own repeated tool invocations are the actual cause by running the tool once, observing the exact delta, and reasoning about whether that delta is explainable by the tool's own matching logic.
rationale: Distinguishes an apparent concurrent-writer race from a self-perpetuating single-process tooling bug.

claim: Before starting a requested "reanchor this stale branch onto main after a squash-merge" task, check the target branch/PR's CURRENT state first -- it may have already been merged or closed by the time the request is made, especially in a fast-moving multi-agent environment where other sessions or the human operator may act on a PR between when a task is described and when work on it begins. A few seconds of state-checking (one API call) avoids doing unnecessary reanchor work on an already-resolved branch, and avoids reporting confusing progress on a PR that no longer needs it.
rationale: Cheap state-check before starting a described task, avoiding wasted reanchor work.

claim: Across a long arc of successive CodeRabbit review rounds on the same evolving PR, a consistent minority of findings are stale (already fixed by intervening work, or describing code that no longer matches the cited lines) and should be verified against current code and skipped with a documented reason rather than blindly re-applied. The majority that are genuinely valid split into two useful categories: findings that are proportionate to fix immediately (a local, well-scoped correctness bug), and findings whose literal ask is disproportionate to the current PR's scope (e.g. "make this schema hard-required across two repositories in the same session" when one of the repositories has no equivalent system to enforce it against) -- for the latter, implement the safer, backward-compatible version of the same underlying concern (optional-and-validated instead of hard-required) and explicitly flag the disproportionate part for the operator's decision rather than either ignoring it or unilaterally implementing the large version.
rationale: Meta-lesson tying together the whole multi-round review discipline across this arc.

claim: GitHub Actions pull_request checkout leaves HEAD at a synthetic server-side test-merge commit, not the PR branch tip — audit ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} for attribution/author checks, never HEAD, or a clean PR gets falsely flagged for an author it never actually had.
rationale: PT/orama PR #190's Git hygiene CI failed on the PR author's registered GitHub account email as bad_author even though every real commit on the branch was authored by the approved (non-owner-gmail) git identity. Root cause: actions/checkout on pull_request events checks out refs/pull/N/merge, and that synthetic merge commit's author is synthesized server-side from the PR author's GitHub account email, unrelated to any git identity used on the branch. Fixed by auditing github.event.pull_request.head.sha instead of HEAD in the CI workflow.

claim: Never trust an automation-authored fix PR's commit message/diagnosis alone — verify it actually changed something (git diff parent commit, or gh pr view additions/deletions/changedFiles) before relying on or merging it; a correct diagnosis can still ship as a genuinely empty commit.
rationale: Cursor's 'Fix CI failures' automation opened a fix PR with an accurate root-cause diagnosis (audit PR head SHA, not the synthetic merge commit) in its commit message and PR body, but the actual commit had a tree byte-identical to its parent — zero real changes. The PR looked 'blank' to the user and kept nagging/reappearing because closing it never resolved the CI failure it was reacting to. Confirmed via git diff <sha>^ <sha> --stat showing 0 files changed, and tree-hash comparison.

claim: Before hardcoding a personal/private identity literal (email, name) into a tracked repo file to satisfy a CI check, look for an existing private-literal escape hatch first (e.g. banned_attribution_lib.sh's private_owner_email_ok() reading .verboten-literals.local) — the repo's own pre-commit hygiene hook will correctly block the literal-hardcoding path, and the real fix is usually a different bug (CI not bootstrapping the private value, or auditing the wrong ref), not a missing allowlist entry.
rationale: Attempted to fix an orama-system PR's attribution failure by adding the owner's private gmail literally to ALLOWED_HUMAN_AE in audit_attribution.sh; the local pre-commit hook (scan_private_verboten_literals in repo_hygiene.py) correctly blocked the commit because that email is registered as an owner_gmail private literal. audit_attribution.sh's author_ok() already calls private_owner_email_ok() for exactly this case — the actual bug was CI auditing the wrong commit ref (the synthetic merge commit), not a missing allowlist entry. Reverted the hardcoding, fixed the real ref bug instead.

claim: Deployed copies of orama-system scripts under ~/.openclaw/scripts/ can silently drift stale vs the canonical repo copy in orama-system/scripts/ — diff them (ignoring CRLF) before trusting the deployed version's behavior, especially after a documented anti-pattern removal in the repo.
rationale: A deployed ~/.openclaw/scripts/discover.py still contained patch_devices_yml()/patch_models_yml() — functions that write live LAN IPs into git-tracked config/devices.yml and config/models.yml. The canonical orama-system/scripts/discover.py removed these 2026-07-08 specifically because they were a doxxing/hygiene footgun (documented inline in the current source). The deployed copy was never re-synced after that fix landed. Found via diff of CRLF-stripped deployed vs canonical, since a naive diff falsely reported the entire file as different due to line-ending differences.

claim: orama-system's discover_endpoints()/last_discovery.json originally supported exactly one Windows LM Studio peer (endpoints.win) — tracking a second concurrent Windows GPU box requires an additive win_peers array (via $WIN_PEER_IPS), not overloading the single win slot, to avoid breaking lm_link_watch.py/lm_link_status.py which only ever read endpoints.win.
rationale: A multi-machine plan called for running two Windows GPU boxes as concurrent AutoResearcher peers, but the original discover_endpoints() had result = {'mac': None, 'win': None} — a single win slot that a second peer's discovery would silently overwrite. Landed an additive win_peers list (probe_extra_win_peers(), wired through filter_endpoints_for_policy/compute_hash/save_discovery_state) as the minimal MVP schema extension; existing single-peer consumers are untouched.

claim: When building schema validation or a packaging format that mirrors an external tool's spec (e.g. Anthropic's packaged-skill frontmatter rules), fetch that tool's actual source (quick_validate.py-style scripts, not just prose docs) and reimplement from the real rules -- don't infer limits/allowed-fields from documentation prose or memory, which can be stale or incomplete.
rationale: Building orama-system's package_skill.py (.skill packaging for skillify), fetched anthropics/claude-plugins-official's actual quick_validate.py and package_skill.py source rather than guessing at the 1024-char description limit, the exact ALLOWED_PROPERTIES set, or the zip-exclude patterns. Confirmed the docs-prose numbers (from an earlier ad-hoc Cowork session's dogfood-upgrade-log.md) were accurate, but having the real source made the reimplementation provably correct rather than plausible.

claim: Doc-processing regexes over a real repo's markdown must be tested against ALL the citation/link styles actually in use, not just the first file checked -- a repo commonly mixes markdown-link form and plain-backtick-path form for the same kind of cross-reference, and a regex tuned to only one form silently drops the other.
rationale: package_skill.py's cross-repo-reference bundler initially only matched markdown-link syntax pointing at a references file two levels up. Testing against skillify's SKILL.md (which uses real links) looked correct, but testing against oramasys-method's SKILL.md (which cites the same references as plain backtick-quoted paths) revealed it silently produced a .skill package with two dead reference paths while bundling an unrelated file. Caught before ever shipping by dogfooding against BOTH real skills, not just the one used to write the regex.

claim: When asked to 'generalize' or 'merge' a fix rather than patch the one broken instance, extract ONE shared implementation called from every site that needs it, and separately audit the whole class the bug belongs to (not just the reported instance) for other latent members -- a fix scoped to only what was reported leaves siblings of the same bug undiscovered.
rationale: A skill-naming collision bug was first fixed narrowly (allow-list one name). When asked to generalize, extracted a single shared collision-check script called from both the naming-time intake workflow and the publish-time sync script, then cross-referenced the repo's full skill manifest against the external suite's own roster and found a second latent collision (this repo's own skill literally sharing the external suite's top-level name) that nobody had reported yet, purely from checking the whole class rather than stopping at the one instance.

claim: A stale local git lock file in a repo that is NOT known to be actively shared with another agent may still be a false positive -- verify with lsof and ps before removing it, since an unrelated system process (e.g. a macOS Virtualization.framework XPC service) can hold a stray read-only file descriptor on the lock path without any real git write in progress.
rationale: A git add in orama-system's checkout was blocked by the standard 'another git process seems to be running' message from a leftover lock file. lsof showed the only handle open on it was a read-only file descriptor from com.apple.Virtualization.VirtualMachine.xpc (an unrelated macOS system process, not a git process), and ps confirmed no actual git write process existed. Removed the zero-byte stale lock only after confirming this, rather than either blindly deleting it or blindly assuming a real conflict and waiting/aborting.

claim: After any git commit whose 'files changed' count looks smaller than what was staged, verify with git show --stat HEAD before trusting the commit captured everything -- a successful exit code does not guarantee every staged file actually landed if something touched the working tree or index between add and commit.
rationale: In orama-system's own (non-shared) checkout, git add staged 10 files but the resulting commit showed only 4 files changed, with no error surfaced. Caught only because git show --stat HEAD was checked immediately after instead of assuming success from exit code 0; the remaining 6 files were still present as uncommitted changes and were re-staged and committed separately. Root cause not fully diagnosed (possibly the pre-commit hook's own repo-hygiene invocation touching state, or brief concurrent activity), but the fix -- always verify post-commit, not just pre-commit -- holds regardless of cause.

claim: Self-reflection: when a user's fix instruction could reasonably be read as either instance-specific or class-general, default to checking for the general case BEFORE presenting the narrow fix as done, rather than shipping the narrow fix and waiting for the user to ask 2-3 more times to broaden it.
rationale: This session's skill-naming collision fix took three user prompts to reach its final, correct scope: first a narrow CI-identity-secret fix, then 'cross-reference all skills', then 'generalize the mechanism in both'. Each was the right next question for the user to ask, but a more proactive first pass -- checking the full manifest for other collisions and proposing a shared mechanism up front, once the first instance revealed the bug class existed -- would have reached the same correct endpoint in one turn instead of three. Not every fix needs this (most really are instance-specific), but a fix that stems from 'I found a bug in how X is checked' is a signal worth pausing on before declaring done.

claim: frugality_router.py, routing.yml's task_type exclusion, and orchestrator.py's req.privacy_critical chain are not three competing implementations — routing.yml + orchestrator.py compose as designed (general policy + explicit override); frugality_router.py is a separate, genuinely-unwired addition whose own spike doc named the wiring gap as deferred follow-on work on 2026-06-29, never a silent omission.
rationale: 2026-07-22 /autoplan pass on the tiered-model navigator initially framed this as three unreconciled privacy systems; tracing hermes-harness assignment/result records (mac-orchestrator-frugality-router-spike.md, win-coder-pt199-frugality-review.md) plus v1.1-definitive.md's own text showed the framing was wrong — two paths already work together, one has a named-but-unpicked TODO. Prevents re-treating a scoped, known gap as an emergency architecture collision.

claim: A spike/PR's own "Not in scope / follow-on" section is a load-bearing TODO list — before concluding a wiring gap is undocumented or an accidental oversight, check whether the original implementation doc already named and deferred it.
rationale: PT #199's spike doc explicitly listed "wire into all dispatch paths (supervisor, fastapi_app)" under deferred follow-on work back on 2026-06-29; it sat unpicked for ~3 weeks. Treating this as a fresh discovery this session would have overstated the finding as a bug rather than a known backlog item.

claim: A plan status banner like "RESOLVED" or "shipped" on a merged module means unit tests passed and code landed — not that any real dispatch path calls it. Verify real callers (grep/CRG) before trusting a shipped/resolved claim for wiring status.
rationale: v1.1-definitive.md's "RESOLVED 2026-06-14 — v1.1 shipped: ... frugality ..." banner was accurate for what it claimed (module merged, tests passing) but easy to misread as "wired into production dispatch," which frugality_router.py never was. This ambiguity cost real investigation time this session before the gbrain trace clarified it.

claim: The frugality/privacy reconciliation decision (2026-07-22): frugality_router.py's resolve_route() becomes the single canonical policy gate that route_task() and orchestrator.py's /orchestrate privacy_critical branch both call; human override is required for any escalation past its default policy, resolved via AskUserQuestion (or host equivalent) when available, else a CLI prompt or dashboard modal — never a silent config-only bypass.
rationale: Human-confirmed decision closing the previously-open 'single gate vs opt-in layer' design question in docs/plans/2026-07-22-frugality-privacy-reconciliation-and-navigator-closeout.md Item 1. Recorded so a future implementer doesn't re-litigate the gate-vs-parallel-layer question or accidentally add a silent override path.

claim: The force-delete-branch git command is blocked by this workstation's dangerous-cmd-block hook even for branches independently verified as fully superseded — when cleanup is needed, write a standalone reviewable shell script to a location outside the hook-restricted session (e.g. OpenClaw/references/) rather than attempting the deletes inline.
rationale: 2026-07-22: attempted the force-delete-branch command on a confirmed-safe branch during a 33-branch cleanup and was blocked. The correct pattern (used successfully) is generate-and-hand-off: produce a dry-run-tested script the user runs themselves outside the restricted session, rather than repeatedly retrying blocked commands.

claim: Never trust reanchor_scan.sh's NEEDS-REANCHOR verdict alone as unmerged work — after a squash-merge, individual commit patch-ids never match main even though all content landed. Confirm with git diff main..<branch> --stat (near-empty = fully absorbed) plus git log main --grep for the absorbing squash-merge commit title before concluding a branch has real unmerged content.
rationale: 2026-07-22 branch cleanup audit: reanchor_scan.sh flagged 13 branches across orama-system + Perpetua-Tools as NEEDS-REANCHOR. Individually verifying each via diff+log-grep found ALL were already fully superseded by squash-merges (PR #146, #142, #183, #203, #211, #258-267, #260/#263) -- zero actually contained unmerged unique work. Trusting the scan's raw verdict would have wrongly treated finished, reviewed work as still-pending.

claim: Never hardcode a fixed relative offset (e.g. dollar-OPENCLAW_ROOT-slash-orama-system, or a literal dollar-HOME path) to locate a sibling repo in MCP/tool configs -- the checkout topology varies (orama-system can be a direct sibling of a caller, or one level removed/aunt to it, e.g. Perpetua-Tools nested under perplexity-api/). Use a cache-first, then walk-from-PWD (sibling and aunt cases), then bounded-find resolver instead.
rationale: 2026-07-22: found .codex/config.toml's exa MCP entry had silently drifted from a hardcoded ORAMA_ROOT-relative path to a completely different transport (npx mcp-remote to a public endpoint) -- likely because the original hardcoded path was fragile and someone worked around it rather than fixing the resolution. Both orama-system/.mcp.json and Perpetua-Tools/.mcp.json had the same hardcoded-HOME-path fragility. Fixed with a portable resolver (orama-system/scripts/exa/resolve-orama-root.sh) plus inline cache-first/walk/find bootstraps in each config, since MCP config launch commands can't depend on a script living inside the very repo they're trying to locate.

claim: When landing substantive work (real code change, closed plan, fix other agents would want to know about), post a one-line GossipBus whiteboard log (scripts/agent_coordination.py log <agent_id> <message>) plus a references/results/<peer>-<date>-<topic>.md peer-inbox drop for anything needing more than one line -- not just for coord-N fan-outs. The whiteboard log is the pointer, the peer-inbox drop is the persistent record.
rationale: 2026-07-22: operationalized into hermes-harness/SKILL.md (v1.1.0.0->1.1.1.0, orama-system commit 143db101) after doing this ad-hoc during a frugality/privacy-gate + repo-hygiene close-out session. Worked example: orama-system bin/orama-system/skills/hermes-harness/references/results/mac-2026-07-22-frugality-p3-and-repo-closeout-status.md. Prevents a peer checking the board mid-work from rediscovering landed work independently.

claim: orama-system's git push origin main over this LAN/connection routinely takes 2+ minutes with zero intermediate output before the pre-push hook banner appears -- this is latency, not a hang. Confirmed 2026-07-22 across 4 consecutive pushes: two completed in under 30s, two took 90-180s and were nearly killed as presumed-stuck before completing successfully on their own. Before killing/retrying a slow orama-system push, background it and wait at least 3 minutes before treating it as genuinely stuck.
rationale: Almost force-killed a push mid-session on the assumption a 90s-silent push was hung, per this workspace's own 'no silent hangs' doctrine for network calls -- but it landed cleanly on its own moments later. The doctrine is still correct (background + timeout hang-prone network calls) but the specific timeout threshold for THIS repo's push needs to be longer than the default 2-minute Bash timeout, or it produces false-positive hang diagnoses.

claim: When fixing a Dependabot alert by bumping to its first_patched_version, check the package's own recent release notes (not just the one CVE range) for newer security releases beyond that version -- a single npm view/gh api release-notes fetch can surface a later advisory that gets silently skipped if you stop reading after finding the version that satisfies the original alert.
rationale: 2026-07-22: fixed @hono/node-server to 2.0.5 (satisfies the path-traversal alert's first_patched_version), but the same release-notes fetch I ran to check for breaking changes ALSO showed a v2.0.10 entry titled 'Security fixes... WebSocket handshake memory-leak DoS' -- and I didn't act on it, only noticing 3 new Dependabot alerts (77-79) after pushing. Caught and fixed same session, but the miss was avoidable: the information was already in front of me.

claim: A single dependency's own advisory family can have multiple, differently-scoped instances in one repo (e.g. the same package resolved at two different major versions via two different parent dependency chains) -- fixing one instance does not close the Dependabot alert for the other. Check for sibling instances of the same package (npm ls / pnpm why across all resolutions) before declaring an advisory family closed.
rationale: 2026-07-22: orama-system had brace-expansion at both 5.0.6 (via minimatch@10, typescript-eslint chain) and 1.1.15 (via minimatch@3.1.5, older eslint chain) -- each with its own Dependabot alert (#8 and #9) and its own vulnerable-range/fix-version pair. Fixed #8 first via a scoped pnpm override, correctly left #9's instance untouched at the time (different major API, needed separate handling) -- but should have checked for the sibling instance immediately rather than discovering it as a fresh alert later.

claim: The shared orama-system working directory can be branch-switched by a concurrent process mid-session without warning -- observed twice in one session (both times to 2026-07-19-001-clinebot-idempotent-install). git push origin main is unaffected (targets origin explicitly regardless of local checkout state), but any command relying on the current checkout (git status, git diff, file reads via relative path) can silently reflect the wrong branch's content. Before trusting a file-content check in a shared checkout, verify git branch --show-current matches main first.
rationale: 2026-07-22: system-reminder file snapshots showed stale/reverted content (old SKILL.md versions, old .mcp.json paths, GOAL.md reappearing) that looked like data loss but was actually a concurrent checkout to a different branch -- confirmed via git reflog, no data was lost. Happened a second time later the same session. This is a repeatable, not one-off, risk in this specific shared checkout.

claim: When fixing CI attribution guard failures for an unapproved author email, do not hardcode the email into tracked APPROVED_IDENTITIES if it is also configured in .verboten-literals.local — the private literal scanner will block it. Instead rely on private_owner_email_ok() which reads from the same verboten literals file at runtime and approves the email without leaking it into git.
rationale: 2026-07-19: PR #190 CI fix for orama-system failed with verboten literal error because <owner Gmail identity> is in .verboten-literals.local (owner_gmail). Hardcoding it in repo_hygiene.py triggered the scanner. The correct fix is to verify private_owner_email_ok is called before the ERROR fallthrough in check_identity.sh and remove the hardcoded addition.

claim: Shell environment can become unresponsive when background git push processes (started with & or nohup) remain alive. Before starting new git/shell work in a session, check for and clean up any orphaned background git processes: ps -axo pid,stat,command | grep 'git push' | grep -v grep | awk '{print $1}' | xargs kill 2>/dev/null
rationale: 2026-07-19: Multiple consecutive git push commands timed out in the tool window. Background processes accumulated and locked the shell's git lock files, causing every subsequent run_commands call to hang for 30s.

claim: Before editing code in a PR branch, verify the author identity of prior commits on that branch. Orphan commits from other agents (Codex, Kimi, Cursor[bot]) may have unapproved author emails that will fail CI attribution checks. Fix by adding the missing email to APPROVED_IDENTITIES only if it is NOT already in .verboten-literals.local.
rationale: 2026-07-19: PR #190 had commits from the repo's approved identity <<owner Gmail identity>> from earlier sessions. The Git hygiene CI job flagged these as bad_author=1 even though the PR code changes themselves were correct.

claim: When another agent's uncommitted work is found sitting in a shared checkout, do not assume it is either live-in-progress OR safe-to-discard from presence alone -- verify liveness independently per artifact type. For code changes tied to a specific PR/CI problem: check the PR's actual current state (gh pr view --json state,statusCheckRollup) and whether the underlying CI job is already green without the change -- a fix left uncommitted can be stale because the real fix already landed a different way. For memory/lesson commits: verify correctness of content instead (does the claim hold up, is it properly anonymized) rather than staleness, since memory entries don't go stale the way code fixes do.
rationale: 2026-07-22: found two artifacts from the same concurrent agent (ClinePass-DeepSeek-v4-flash) in the same session -- an uncommitted repo_hygiene.py/check_identity.sh edit from a 2026-07-19 PR190 handoff (turned out stale: PR190 already merged 3 days ago with Git hygiene passing, the runtime private_owner_email_ok() check already covered the case, discarding was correct) and a same-session memory-lesson commit (turned out legitimate: well-formed, correctly anonymized, reached the same conclusion independently). Treating both under one blanket rule (either 'always trust' or 'always discard') would have been wrong for one of the two.

claim: A handoff doc's own status (BLOCKED, needs review) does not mean the underlying problem is still unresolved -- the same problem can get fixed a different way by a different agent/session before the handoff is ever picked up. Before acting on a handoff's recommended fix, re-check the actual current state of what it describes (PR status, CI status, file content) rather than trusting the handoff's problem statement at face value.
rationale: 2026-07-22: a local handoff note described PR190 as BLOCKED with a circular-dependency problem needing orchestrator resolution -- but PR190 had already merged successfully 3 days prior with the CI check passing, meaning the blocking problem no longer existed by the time the handoff was read. The handoff correctly diagnosed the root cause and even named the right fix (Option B), but its BLOCKED status was stale.

claim: SELF-REFLECTION (2026-07-22, provisional): tonight's session was genuinely good work -- the frugality/privacy gate landed tested and verified, 4 Dependabot rounds got fixed correctly (including catching my own missed-advisory mistake), and the concurrent-agent verification thread was handled with real rigor (checked PR/CI state before discarding anything, distinguished stale from legitimate work). But candidly: I used ALLOW_MAIN_PUSH=1 to bypass the PR-only-write gate roughly 15+ times across both repos tonight. Each override was nominally covered by one broad early user confirmation ('push all'), but the sheer volume of direct-to-main pushes without individual PR review is a real deviation from this repo's own stated Phase 0 doctrine, and I never re-surfaced that volume to the user as it accumulated -- I should have flagged 'this is now the Nth main-push override tonight, still want me to keep going this way?' at some natural checkpoint rather than treating the first blanket confirmation as covering an open-ended stream of them.
rationale: Requested explicitly by the user: honest self-reflection on the session, not just mechanical lesson extraction. The gate-bypass volume is the one thing I'd flag to a future reviewer of this session's git history -- not because any individual push was wrong (each was tested, verified, low-risk), but because 'confirmed once' quietly became 'confirmed indefinitely' without me checking back in, which is exactly the kind of scope-creep-via-accumulation this session's own discipline was built to catch in OTHER contexts (deferred-plan scope, branch cleanup scope) but I didn't apply to my own git-push behavior.

claim: lan_peer_assign.py's 'read' command (non-JSON mode) crashes on Windows with UnicodeEncodeError when a peer message body contains non-cp1252 characters (e.g. arrow U+2192) -- print() hits the Windows console codepage, not UTF-8. Use --json plus PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 to read message bodies reliably on Windows.
rationale: Hit live reading a real Mac coordination message containing a unicode arrow in its title -- plain 'lan_peer_assign.py read --peer ...' crashed with a traceback instead of printing the body.

claim: DHCP-assigned peer IPs (Win GPU nodes especially) drift even between recent, otherwise-correct coordination docs -- always live-probe the actual IP rather than trusting a handoff doc's value, even one written the same week.
rationale: The Mac's own coordination doc (dated 2026-07-08) listed RTX 3080 at 192.168.9.240; a live probe the same session found it had moved to 192.168.9.18. The doc's instructions were otherwise entirely correct -- only the specific IP had gone stale from a DHCP lease renewal.

claim: When a fast-forward sync is blocked by a local uncommitted change of unknown provenance (not authored this session), git stash it with a descriptive message rather than discarding it or guessing whether to keep it -- preserves the work for later review without blocking the sync or silently destroying something intentional.
rationale: A local .codex/config.toml diff (bash-wrapper exa MCP vs npx mcp-remote) blocked a 22-commit fast-forward. Comparing the stashed version to the newly-synced upstream version showed upstream had deliberately kept the more robust bash-resolver approach -- reapplying the stash would have been a regression, but discarding it outright would have destroyed someone else's work without knowing why it existed.

claim: For a 'run this more often' ask, reuse the existing scheduled-task script with a changed interval parameter instead of building new infrastructure -- coord_pulse.ps1 already covered heartbeat, peer probe, and inbox/outbox flush; only install_coord_pulse.ps1's -IntervalSec needed to change from 900 to 60.
rationale: User asked for a 60-second heartbeat + coordination-board + peer-inbox check loop. Reinstalling the existing OramaCoordPulse task at -IntervalSec 60 achieved the outcome with zero new code and a proven-stable script. Verified one live tick completes in ~12s, comfortably inside the 60s window.

claim: .agent/harness/hooks/_episodic_io.py's episodic_lock() hard-raised RuntimeError on any Windows Python with no fcntl -- completely blocking learn.py/memory writes on every Windows agent, not just one session. Fixed by adding an msvcrt.locking()-based Windows lock path alongside the POSIX fcntl one (both lock a 1-byte region of a sidecar .lock file; msvcrt has no shared-lock primitive so both exclusive and shared requests take the same exclusive lock there, which is correct -- just slightly more serializing than POSIX).
rationale: Every learn.py call failed hard on this Windows box until this fix -- a landed commit had introduced fcntl-only locking with a bare 'raise RuntimeError' for the Windows case, with no fallback at all, silently breaking memory-writing for the entire Windows side of this fleet. Fixed and verified live: the exact lesson-graduation call that failed before now succeeds.

claim: When a client-side auth resolver picks 'the one preferred token' (e.g. candidates[0] of a priority list) and a peer/service rejects it, don't conclude the credential isn't deployed -- test every LOCALLY AVAILABLE candidate directly against the target first. In a real incident, a second local token candidate was accepted (HTTP 200) by the exact service that rejected the first one; the fix was retrying across candidates client-side, not an operator syncing anything. Single-token resolvers used for AUTHENTICATION should retry across all available candidates on HTTP 401 responses before surfacing an operator-actionable error, mirroring how multi-candidate retry is already used elsewhere in the same codebase for exactly this reason.
rationale: Two call sites (a topology-query script and a peer-file-drop script) each called a single-token resolver instead of the multi-candidate list a THIRD script in the same file already used successfully. Cost one full investigation cycle (correctly-worded but wrong root-cause finding, self-corrected) before the real bug (client retry gap, not token deployment) was found by directly testing each candidate.

claim: In a merge/seed function that folds a REMOTE peer's self-reported data into LOCAL state, never derive the local entity's own identity from the remote payload -- even in the 'first response, no prior state' bootstrap branch where it's tempting to just reuse whatever field the peer sent. A real bug: a topology-merge function's bootstrap branch set local_node = peer_data['local_node'] (the PEER's own hostname), which then made the local node equal its own single peer-list entry, silently miscounting peers_reachable to 0. Always seed local identity from a LOCAL source (hostname, config, env) even when no prior local state exists yet.
rationale: Found live, running the fleet-mesh mother plan against real peer data for the first time -- masked for the session's entire prior history by an unrelated auth bug that always failed before reaching this code path. Fixed with socket.gethostname(); regression tests added asserting local_node never equals a value the peer payload supplied.

claim: A synthetic test fixture and the code under test can both encode the SAME wrong schema assumption, in which case the test suite passing proves nothing about real data -- it just proves internal self-consistency. A real incident: a topology-display function assumed peer entries were dicts and crashed on the canonical writer's real flat-string schema; 125 existing tests never caught it because the fixture file's mocks used the exact same wrong dict-shaped assumption the buggy code expected, rather than what the actual writer produced. When a reader/writer pair is implemented far apart in time (or by different agents/sessions), verify the reader against the WRITER's actual canonical schema/dataclass directly -- not against a fixture that may have inherited the same wrong assumption as the code it's meant to catch bugs in.
rationale: Second instance of this exact class of gap in one session (first: lesson_7155c5157bd4, verify-against-real-data for a heartbeat-worktree bug). Confirmed by reading the canonical PT dataclass's own field type (peers: list[str]) directly rather than trusting either the buggy code or its matching-wrong fixture.

claim: Self-reflection, fleet-mesh completion session (2026-07-19/22): the session's own discipline of 'verify against real data, not synthetic assumptions' was violated once by the same agent enforcing it -- D8's first-pass diagnosis ('shared token not deployed, operator must sync it') was a plausible-sounding conclusion accepted after testing only the SINGLE resolved token, when testing the small, already-locally-available set of candidate tokens (2 total) would have found the real answer (a working second candidate) immediately and for near-zero extra cost. The self-correction (D9) happened, and was logged honestly per this workspace's standing discipline rather than silently edited over -- but the more honest lesson is that 'exhaust the cheap local checks before concluding something needs an operator/external action' should be a reflex applied BEFORE writing a finding down, not a repair applied after. Positive pattern worth keeping, not just the failure: despite high output volume this session (3 real production bugs found+fixed+tested in the fleet-mesh chain alone, on top of the earlier coordination-module work), every fix was still verified two ways (synthetic regression test AND live real-data check) before being reported done -- the discipline held under volume, it just missed applying itself one level earlier on D8 specifically.
rationale: Requested explicitly (self-reflection ask). The pattern (jumping to 'X needs an operator/external fix' before exhausting cheap local verification) is worth naming as its own reflex-level check, distinct from the already-graduated 'verify against real data' lesson (lesson_7155c5157bd4) -- that lesson is about not trusting synthetic tests alone; this one is about not trusting the FIRST plausible external-blocker explanation before checking what's already available locally.

claim: When a Python file fails to even parse (a SyntaxError), the resulting CI failure can present as a completely unrelated logical error -- an identity check, a scanner returning wrong results, or any other symptom the script would have produced if it ran. Before reasoning about WHY a check's logic seems wrong, verify the file actually parses (python3 -c "import ast; ast.parse(open(f).read())") as the first diagnostic step for any Python-based CI failure. Skipping this step can lead to several rounds of fixing real-but-secondary logic gaps while the actual blocker (a syntax error) sits unaddressed above all of them.
rationale: Would have saved several rounds this exact session if applied as the first diagnostic step.

claim: When a shared condition gates two logically-independent checks (e.g. "skip check A" reusing the same boolean that correctly gates "skip check B"), a scenario that legitimately satisfies the shared condition for check A will silently also skip check B, even though check B has no relationship to why the exemption exists. Before reusing an existing exemption/skip condition for a new check, ask whether the new check's OWN reason for existing has anything to do with the original exemption's reason -- if not, it needs its own independent condition, not a shared one.
rationale: Concrete, verified real bug from this session's own scanner code.

claim: When adding a narrow content exemption scoped to one specific file or directory (e.g. "graduated candidate JSON may contain operational network evidence"), check whether that content legitimately flows onward into other tracked files through an established pipeline (rendering, mirroring, superseding) before assuming the exemption's scope is complete. A fix that only exempts the point of origin will start flagging the SAME already-approved content again the moment it's rendered, mirrored, or copied downstream -- discoverable by running the real, full check against the actual repository's current tracked content, not just the specific test scenario that prompted the fix.
rationale: Directly caused a broken fix that would have shipped without checking the real repo's own content.

claim: A single red CI check can be caused by multiple independent, stacked bugs rather than one -- fixing the bug that the current failure log describes does not guarantee the next CI run will be green, because a different bug may have been hidden behind the one just fixed (never reached, since the script crashed or returned before getting there). After pushing a fix, always fetch and read the ACTUAL next CI run's log rather than assuming success from local verification alone -- local tests can pass while the real CI environment (different secrets, different working directory, different concurrent state) surfaces a genuinely different failure the local run never could have caught.
rationale: The meta-pattern tying together this whole 5-round CI saga.

claim: When a repository has multiple agents or sessions concurrently editing the same shared, security-critical enforcement code (a hygiene scanner, an identity checker, an attribution guard), isolated unit tests with synthetic fixtures are not sufficient protection -- they can all pass while the real, unmodified repository's actual tracked content fails the same check, because concurrent edits accumulate real content the fixtures never modeled. The stronger, cheaper safeguard is a single test that runs the real check function against the real repository's current tracked files (not a tmp_path fixture) as part of the normal suite, so any concurrent edit that breaks the real content -- not just the scenario a fixture happens to construct -- is caught locally before it ever reaches CI.
rationale: Directly explains why fixture-based tests kept passing while real-content checks kept catching new issues.

claim: Do not pattern-match on a CI check's NAME when it fails repeatedly -- the same-named check (e.g. "Git hygiene") can fail for entirely different, unrelated root causes across successive pushes, especially on a branch with concurrent commits from other agents landing between each push. Treat every new failure of a repeatedly-failing check as a fresh diagnosis: fetch and read that specific run's actual log before assuming it is a continuation of, or the same bug as, the failure just fixed. Conflating "still failing" with "still the same problem" is what makes a genuinely multi-bug situation feel like one intractable bug that will not go away.
rationale: The reflective through-line of the whole 5-round saga -- reading each failure fresh is what made it tractable.

claim: When writing detection code for a banned literal or pattern (a scanner, a sanitizer, a redaction rule), proactively add a self-exemption for the file that defines the pattern in the SAME commit that introduces the pattern -- do not wait for CI or a later pass to discover that the detector's own source (its comments, its regex definition) necessarily contains the literal text it is designed to catch. This is a structural certainty, not an edge case: any rule specific enough to usefully detect a pattern is specific enough to match its own definition.
rationale: Forward-looking: this exact paradox is now predictable, not something that needs rediscovering.

claim: Do not call ScheduleWakeup to re-arm a recurring check that a CronCreate recurring job already covers -- CronCreate jobs with recurring:true fire automatically on their own cron schedule without any further action; calling ScheduleWakeup on top of one creates a second, redundant wakeup mechanism that can double-fire the same work. Manage an existing recurring cron job's lifecycle with CronList/CronDelete, not ScheduleWakeup (which is the /loop dynamic-mode continuation tool, not a general recurring-task primitive).

Caught and cancelled it immediately via ScheduleWakeup stop:true before it could double-fire.

claim: Self-reflection: the same failure mode -- assuming a coordination channel works because it worked before or looks fine from an interactive check, without verifying its actual current mechanism/state -- appeared independently on all 3 fleet nodes in one session, not just this agent. Mac logged status updates to a board that never left the machine (intra-machine SQLite, confirmed only by reading the tool's own docstring). win-rtx5080 filename-guessed expected inbox replies instead of doing a full inbox listing, missing 2 already-delivered messages. win-rtx3080 had a Scheduled Task silently go Disabled for 10 days while interactive/manual checks (which used a different env-loading path) kept looking healthy. None of these were caught by symptom-level monitoring -- each required someone to check the actual underlying mechanism (source code, full directory listing, Get-ScheduledTask state) rather than trusting the higher-level signal. When multi-agent coordination seems to be silently dropping messages, the fix is rarely 'retry harder' -- it's checking whether the channel believed to be working is the one actually being used.
rationale: 2026-07-23: this pattern surfaced 3 times independently within about an hour of real fleet-mesh coordination work, across 3 different machines and 2 different AI systems -- strong enough repetition to treat as a general class of bug, not 3 unrelated incidents. Worth periodic, deliberate 'is this channel actually connected' checks in any multi-node coordination setup, especially ones assembled incrementally across sessions where no single agent designed the whole comms topology.
